Reference architecture · AWS

Nobody waits on the order.
The queue does the waiting.

A mobile customer places an order. Instead of making them sit through fulfillment in real time, the request is dropped onto a queue and acknowledged instantly — a second function processes it in the background, and only the outcome comes back around.

Fig. 01 — request & message flowAsync · Decoupled · Retry-safe
What actually happens

Six handoffs, one decoupled pipeline

Every stage only knows about the one next to it. That's what lets the queue absorb a burst of orders, and what lets a failing message get pulled aside instead of stalling everything behind it.

01

Order submitted

Customer places an order from the mobile app; the request hits API Gateway as a POST to /orders.

02

Queued, not processed

CreateOrder writes the order straight onto Amazon SQS and returns immediately — the customer isn't kept waiting on fulfillment.

03

Picked up async

ProcessOrder is triggered by the queue one message at a time and does the actual fulfillment work in the background.

04a

Success path

Processing succeeds → ProcessOrder publishes to Amazon SNS → the customer gets an email confirming the order.

04b

Failure path

Processing fails three times → the redrive policy moves the message to the Dead Letter Queue instead of retrying forever.

05

Nothing is lost

Every order either reaches the customer as a confirmation, or lands somewhere visible for a human to inspect.

Build sequence

Nine steps, console-first

Built entirely from the AWS console, in the order the pipeline depends on itself — the queue exists before anything can send to it, the role exists before the functions that need it.

01
Create the SQS queue

This is where every incoming order lands before anything touches it.

Name order-queue
Type Standard
Visibility timeout 30 sec
Retention 4 days
order-queue · configuration
02
Create the Dead Letter Queue

A second, identical queue that only ever receives messages the pipeline gave up on.

Name order-dlq
Type Standard
Visibility timeout 30 sec
Retention 4 days
order-dlq · configuration

Then, back on order-queue, set its Dead Letter Queue to order-dlq with a maximum receive count.

Maximum receives 3
order-queue · redrive policy → order-dlq
If the Lambda consuming a message fails three times, that message moves to the DLQ automatically — no custom retry logic required.
03
Create the SNS topic

The channel that carries the "your order went through" notification out to the customer.

Type Standard
Name order-notification

04
Subscribe an email endpoint

Inside the topic, add a subscription and confirm it from the inbox before it will deliver anything.

Protocol Email
Endpoint your notification address

Lambda source

The two functions, in full

CreateOrder only ever writes to the queue. ProcessOrder only ever reads from it and reports the outcome — neither one knows the other exists.

CreateOrder — receives the request, enqueues the order

create_order.py
import json
import boto3
import os
import uuid

sqs = boto3.client('sqs')
QUEUE_URL = os.environ['QUEUE_URL']

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    body = json.loads(event['body'])
    order = {
        "orderId": str(uuid.uuid4()),
        "customer": body["customer"],
        "product": body["product"],
        "quantity": body["quantity"]
    }

    sqs.send_message(
        QueueUrl=QUEUE_URL,
        MessageBody=json.dumps(order)
    )

    return {
        "statusCode": 200,
        "body": json.dumps({
            "message": "Order Created",
            "order": order
        })
    }

ProcessOrder — consumes the queue, notifies the customer

process_order.py
import json
import boto3
import os

sns = boto3.client('sns')
TOPIC = os.environ['SNS_TOPIC_ARN']

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    for record in event['Records']:
        order = json.loads(record['body'])
        print(order)

        sns.publish(
            TopicArn=TOPIC,
            Subject="Order Successful",
            Message=f"""
Order ID: {order['orderId']}
Customer: {order['customer']}
Product: {order['product']}
Quantity: {order['quantity']}
"""
        )

    return {
        "statusCode": 200,
        "headers": {
            "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*",
            "Access-Control-Allow-Headers": "Content-Type",
            "Access-Control-Allow-Methods": "POST,OPTIONS"
        },
        "body": json.dumps({
            "orderId": order["orderId"]
        })
    }
Note: the original snippet returns order_id outside the loop where it isn't defined — reference order["orderId"] from the last processed record, as shown above, or track it before the loop exits.
